# Engineered roads (Roman roads to macadam) (`paved_roads_macadam`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by surveying_triangulation, lime_burning, spoked_wheel_suspension_carriage
- Core idea: The secret of a road is a dry foundation: raise and camber it, dig side ditches, and the subsoil will carry the load. McAdam's cheap method: a 25 cm layer of small, broken, angular stones no larger than 5 cm (each under about 170 g), laid in thin courses on drained ground; traffic crushes them into a hard, watershedding crust. The Romans used thick layered beds and paving slabs, durable but very expensive.
- Pitfalls:
  - Using round river gravel; it does not interlock
  - Mixing soil or clay into the stone layer, which turns to mud in the rain
  - Neglecting drainage; no surface survives a waterlogged base
  - Thinking medieval Europe had no roads; it had many, mostly unpaved and maintained by local obligation
- History: mesopotamia: 6th–5th c. BC – Persian Royal Road from Susa to Sardis (about 2,500 km); rome: 312 BC – Via Appia; about 80,000 km of main roads by the 2nd c. AD; china: 3rd c. BC – Qin straight roads and standardised axle widths; americas: 15th c. – Inca road network (Qhapaq Ñan), about 40,000 km with suspension bridges; europe: 1764 – Trésaguet in France; 1800s Telford; 1816 McAdam; 1902 tarmac patent (Hooley)
- Read:
  - John Loudon McAdam, Remarks on the Present System of Road Making (1816)
  - M. G. Lay, Ways of the World: A History of the World's Roads and of the Vehicles That Used Them (1992)
